court: Supreme Court (D.Y. Chandrachud and M.R. Shah JJ.)
citation: Civil Appeal No. 1155 of 2021 (arising from SLP (C) No. 1688 of 2021); AIR 2021 SC 2114; (2021) 3 SCR 406 (per the digiscr link). Arose under the HPGST Act.

Once a final s.74(9) order is passed, the attachment ends; on appeal, s.107(6)-(7) govern stay of recovery (para 72(xi)-(xii)). Alternative remedy is a rule of discretion; exceptions are enforcement of a fundamental right, breach of natural justice, proceedings wholly without jurisdiction, or a vires challenge (para 27(iii)). court: Supreme Court (Dinesh Maheshwari and Hrishikesh Roy JJ.)

issue: A-I. Validity of arrest and summons powers, and the safeguards
case: Radhika Agarwal v. Union of India
citation: 2025 INSC 272; (2025) 6 SCC 545; [2025] 2 S.C.R. 1331; 2025 SCC OnLine SC 449. Lead case W.P.(Crl.) No. 336 of 2018 with connected criminal appeals and writ petitions. Three judges: Sanjiv Khanna CJI (main judgment, joined by M.M. Sundresh J) and Bela M. Trivedi J (separate concurring opinion).
holding: Upheld ss.69 and 70 of the CGST Act and the Customs Act arrest powers. "Reasons to believe" must rest on verifiable material and statutory monetary thresholds, not mere suspicion. Final assessment of liability is not a precondition. Written grounds of arrest must be furnished. CrPC/BNSS provisions "are equally applicable" to arrests under the GST and Customs Acts. Anticipatory bail can be sought even without an FIR. A person summoned under s.70 is not, merely by the summons, an accused. The Court also held that s.74(5) "voluntary" payment "does not postulate payment under force, coercion or threat of arrest", that CBIC's circulars on this are binding, and that taxpayers who paid under threat, force or coercion may move the courts for refund (main judgment paras 64-68).
later_history: Followed in Rakesh Kumar v. UoI (SC, 29 Jun 2026) and UoI v. Sunil Biyani (SC, 2026). No review or reversal found.
use_in_orders: Cite for validity of ss.69/70. Arrest files must show material-based reasons recorded in writing, the s.132 threshold, written grounds, and CrPC/BNSS compliance (D.K. Basu, intimation, production before Magistrate within 24 hours).

issue: A-I. Validity of arrest and summons powers, and the safeguards
case: Union of India v. Sunil Biyani
citation: 2026 INSC 849. Criminal Appeal arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 12535 of 2026. Dipankar Datta (author) and Sheel Nagu, JJ. Judgment dated 12 Aug 2026 (other reported dates are wrong). Arose from a Bombay High Court order of 13 Feb 2026 in ABA No. 3001/2025.
holding: A s.69 arrest authorisation, being a "sine qua non to seek anticipatory bail," must be communicated to the person before arrest. It may be served by the email and mobile number given under Rule 8 CGST Rules or another lawful mode. Without communication, "question of arrest would not arise." Communication does not obstruct investigation. Once an anticipatory bail application is dismissed as not maintainable, a High Court or Sessions Court cannot grant independent interim protection. The Bombay High Court's one-week protection was set aside. Rejection of pre-arrest bail at the bare summons stage was affirmed (summons alone does not make a person an accused). The Court added (para 20) that the order is open to judicial review and that withholding the "reasons to believe" "could have drastic consequences on the right to liberty". The operative direction was to the Commissioner in this case, but the reasoning is general.
use_in_orders: Before any arrest, serve the s.69 order and keep proof of service in the file. An arrest on an uncommunicated authorisation is at serious risk.

issue: 3. Part B: Landmark constitutional and levy rulings
case: Torrent Power Ltd. v. Union of India
citation: R/SCA No. 12175 of 2024 and 12 connected SCAs; 2026:GUJHC:51510-DB (neutral citation not seen in the Indian Kanoon text). A.S. Supehia and Vaibhavi D. Nanavati, JJ.

citation: R/SCA No. 1350 of 2021 with SCA Nos. 6840 of 2021 and 5052 of 2022 (DB: J.B. Pardiwala, Nisha M. Thakore JJ).
holding: The mandatory one-third land deduction in para 2 of Notf. 11/2017-CT(Rate) (and the State notification) is ultra vires the GST Acts and violates Art. 14. It was read down, not struck down: the one-third is available only at the taxpayer's option where the actual value of land or undivided share is not ascertainable. Refund with 6% interest was ordered to the petitioner-buyer.
later_history: The Union's SLP(C) No. 21703/2022 (with connected SLPs and W.P.(C) 1382/2023) is pending in the SC without any stay shown in the orders read; on 18.08.2026 it was listed for 07.12.2026.
use_in_orders: Where a builder shows the actual land value (sale deed or guideline value) and asks for it, don't insist on the one-third. Where the notification is applied, record why the actual value can't be ascertained.
verified: Primary - read on Indian Kanoon 14 Oct 2026; "struck down" corrected to "read down" (para 124); bench and case nos. added; pending SLP found (was "no appeal found").

issue: 2. Liquidated damages, notice pay, compensation (Sch. II para 5(e); Circular 178/10/2022)
case: Krazybee Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Additional Director, DGGI
holding: Liquidated damages an NBFC recovered from a lending service provider for breach or delay under a master service agreement are compensation, not consideration for "tolerating an act" under Sch. II para 5(e). The DGGI SCN dated 25.04.2024 was quashed, relying on paras 7.1 to 7.1.6 of Circular 178/10/2022, and refund of Rs 5 crore paid under protest, with interest, was ordered.
use_in_orders: A para 5(e) demand needs evidence of a separate agreement to tolerate. A penalty clause in the main contract is not enough.

issue: 2. Liquidated damages, notice pay, compensation (Sch. II para 5(e); Circular 178/10/2022)
case: GE T&D India Ltd. v. Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise
citation: W.P. Nos. 35728 to 35734 of 2016 (07.11.2019); followed in W.P. No. 26292 of 2018 (13.12.2019). Reporter citations differ: [2020] 119 taxmann.com 55 (Mad.); 2019 (12) TMI 1566; 2020 (1) TMI 1096.

issue: 4. Valuation: reimbursements and pure agent
case: Union of India v. Intercontinental Consultants and Technocrats Pvt. Ltd.
court: Supreme Court (A.K. Sikri, Ashok Bhushan JJ)
citation: Civil Appeal No. 2013 of 2014 with connected appeals and transferred cases (affirms Delhi HC, 2012).
holding: Rule 5(1) of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006 (including reimbursed expenses in value) was ultra vires ss.66/67 Finance Act 1994. Tax is only on the value of the service actually rendered. Reimbursements became includible only after s.67 was amended (14.05.2015), a substantive and not declaratory change. The Revenue's appeals were dismissed.
later_history: Overtaken for GST by s.15(2)(c) CGST Act and rule 33. Still cited for the principle that rules cannot widen the charging section.

case: X'SS Beverage Co. v. State of Assam
citation: W.P.(C) Nos. 5340, 5341, 5342, 5346 and 5347 of 2022 (periods July 2017 to August 2021).

issue: 5. Classification of goods (GST and excise/VAT rulings still applied)
case: Commissioner of Central Excise, Salem v. Madhan Agro Industries (India) Pvt. Ltd.
court: Supreme Court (3 judges: Sanjiv Khanna CJI, Sanjay Kumar, R. Mahadevan JJ)
citation: Civil Appeal No. 1766 of 2009 with C.A. Nos. 6703-6710 of 2009; 2024 INSC 1002 (judgment by Sanjay Kumar J).

issue: 5. Classification of goods (GST and excise/VAT rulings still applied)
case: Addl. Commissioner, Commercial Tax v. Cadila Health Care Ltd.
citation: Civil Appeal Nos. 9788-9789 of 2013; 2026 INSC 1078 (judgment by Manmohan J; appeal from MP HC, W.P. Nos. 3020 and 4633 of 2003, 03.08.2011).
holding: Classification depends on the form of the goods at the time of sale (the taxable event), not on how the consumer later uses them. "GRD Powder" and "GRD Mix" (powder and biscuit form) fell under the residuary entry of the MP Commercial Tax Act 1994, not "non-alcoholic drinks and beverages". Goods not answering a specific entry go to the residuary entry and can't be forced into one for a higher rate. The MP HC was upheld and the appeals dismissed.
use_in_orders: Classify goods as supplied. Don't rely on end use unless the tariff entry itself is end-use based.

case: STS-KEC JV v. State Tax Officer
citation: W.P.(MD) Nos. 3938 to 3942 of 2024 (Madurai Bench).
holding: A works contract from RVNL for railway infrastructure is covered by entry 3(v) of Notf. 11/2017-CT(Rate) (as amended by Notf. 20/2017), Notf. 8/2017-IT(Rate) and the State G.O., and is taxable at 12%, not 18%. The impugned orders were set aside.

issue: 9. Exemptions: interpretation, hostels, education
case: Commissioner of Customs (Import), Mumbai v. Dilip Kumar and Company
citation: Civil Appeal No. 3327 of 2007; AIR 2018 SC 3606 (Ranjan Gogoi, N.V. Ramana, R. Banumathi, Mohan M. Shantanagoudar, S. Abdul Nazeer JJ).
holding: An exemption notification is construed strictly. The burden is on the assessee to show it comes within it, and any ambiguity about eligibility is resolved in favour of the Revenue. Sun Export (1997), which had given the benefit of ambiguity to the assessee, was overruled. The Court also concurred (paras 46-47) with the line that once eligibility is strictly established, the notification may be construed liberally.

The "liberal once eligible" point is in paras 46-47 of the judgment itself (approving Parle Exports: "Do not extend or widen the ambit at stage of applicability. But once that hurdle is crossed, construe it liberally").

issue: 9. Exemptions: interpretation, hostels, education
case: State of Karnataka v. Taghar Vasudeva Ambrish
court: Supreme Court (J.B. Pardiwala, K.V. Viswanathan JJ)
citation: Civil Appeal No. 7846 of 2023 with C.A. No. 7847 of 2023; 2025 INSC 1380 (judgment by J.B. Pardiwala J).
holding: Leasing a residential building to a lessee who runs it as a hostel for students and working professionals is "renting of residential dwelling for use as residence" under entry 13 of Notf. 9/2017-IT(Rate) (12/2017-CT(Rate) equivalent). The exemption does not require the lessee to live there itself. "Residential dwelling" takes its common-parlance meaning, and long-stay hostels differ from hotels and guest houses. domain: Interest, penalty, returns and other procedure
issue: 7. Cross-empowerment and parallel proceedings (s.6(2)(b))
case: Armour Security (India) Ltd v. Commissioner, CGST, Delhi East Commissionerate
court: Supreme Court (J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan JJ.)
citation: 2025 INSC 982; SLP (C) No. 6092 of 2025 (disposed of with conclusions and guidelines; leave not granted). [2025] 177 taxmann.com 478 (SC) and AIR 2025 SC 3854 as reported (not seen on Indian Kanoon).
holding: "Initiation of any proceedings" in s.6(2)(b) means formal adjudicatory proceedings by an SCN; summons, search, seizure and other evidence-gathering are not proceedings (para 96(v)-(vi)). "Subject matter" is the tax liability or obligation from a particular contravention; an identical or partial overlap attracts the bar, but distinct infractions do not, even if the amount is similar. Two-fold test: same liability/offence on the same facts, and identical demand (para 96(vii)-(x)). Audit and detailed-scrutiny action must be initiated by the administration to which the taxpayer is assigned; intelligence-based enforcement can be taken by either, but the other should not start parallel proceedings (para 96(ii)-(iv)). Guidelines (para 97): taxpayer must still comply with summons; must tell the later authority in writing of the overlap; authorities must verify and reply with reasons; an SCN on a liability already covered by an existing SCN "shall be quashed"; if they cannot agree, the authority that started first continues.
later_history: applied by the Delhi HC in Sanskriti Exim and the Sept 2026 DGGI batch.
use_in_orders: investigation can proceed in parallel. Before issuing an SCN, verify that no SCN on the same subject matter has been issued by the other administration, and record that check. Audit and scrutiny of State-assigned taxpayers stay with the State.
